lead: An inverter cannot switch instantly: the output node has capacitance and the transistors supply only limited current. Delay is the time the output takes to reach the 50% point after the input crosses it. Clock frequency, setup slack and hold slack are all built from these delays. This chapter defines t<sub>PHL</sub>, t<sub>PLH</sub>, t<sub>p</sub>, t<sub>r</sub> and t<sub>f</sub>, gives two hand estimates, and lists what loads the node.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.1 for the inverter's voltage transfer curve, and Unit 1 for MOSFET capacitances.

blocks.text: Every delay is measured between 50% crossings. V<sub>DD</sub> is the supply voltage, so the 50% point is V<sub>DD</sub>/2.

items: t<sub>PHL</sub> — output high-to-low: input crosses V<sub>DD</sub>/2 rising, output crosses V<sub>DD</sub>/2 falling. The nMOS pull-down sets it.
t<sub>PLH</sub> — output low-to-high: input crosses V<sub>DD</sub>/2 falling, output crosses it rising. The pMOS pull-up sets it.
t<sub>p</sub> — the average of the two.
t<sub>r</sub> — rise time, output 10% to 90% of V<sub>DD</sub> (some books use 20% to 80%).
t<sub>f</sub> — fall time, output 90% to 10% of V<sub>DD</sub>.

blocks.where: t<sub>PHL</sub>, t<sub>PLH</sub> and t<sub>p</sub> are in seconds (usually ns or ps).

blocks.text: Rise time and delay answer different questions. t<sub>r</sub> describes the shape of one edge; t<sub>p</sub> describes when that edge arrives. A node with a weak resistive pull-up crosses 50% quickly and then crawls up to V<sub>DD</sub>, so its t<sub>r</sub> can be several times its t<sub>p</sub>.
A ring oscillator of N inverters has period 2·N·t<sub>p</sub>, so its frequency is 1/(2·N·t<sub>p</sub>). Measuring that frequency on silicon measures t<sub>p</sub>.

Count the charge. For t<sub>PHL</sub> the output falls from V<sub>DD</sub> to V<sub>DD</sub>/2, so the charge removed is C<sub>L</sub>·V<sub>DD</sub>/2. The nMOS is saturated only until the output reaches V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>; below that it enters the linear region and its current drops. Using the saturation current for the whole half swing gives an optimistic estimate, so the real delay is a little longer.

blocks.where: k<sub>n</sub> = µ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>(W/L) is the nMOS gain in A/V²; V<sub>tn</sub> is the nMOS threshold in V; V<sub>DD</sub> is the supply in V; I<sub>Dsat</sub> is in A. Channel-length modulation is ignored.
C<sub>L</sub> is the total load capacitance in farads, V<sub>DD</sub> in volts, I<sub>Dsat</sub> in amperes; t<sub>PHL</sub> comes out in seconds.

items: Find k<sub>n</sub> and V<sub>tn</sub> from the process data and the drawn W/L.
Compute I<sub>Dsat</sub> from the overdrive V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>.
Add up C<sub>L</sub>: drain diffusions, gate-drain overlaps, wire, and the input capacitance of every fanout gate.
Apply the formula. Repeat with the pMOS current for t<sub>PLH</sub>, then average.

blocks.text: The factor 2 matters: the delay stops at the 50% point, so only half the swing is charged. A full swing to 0 V would take about twice as long, and in practice longer, because the nMOS leaves saturation.
The RC method treats the ON transistor as a resistance R<sub>eq</sub>. The output follows V<sub>DD</sub>(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>) with τ = R<sub>eq</sub>C<sub>L</sub>, and reaches x = 0.5 at t = τ·ln2.

blocks.where: R<sub>eq</sub> is the equivalent ON resistance in Ω (roughly V<sub>DD</sub>/(2·I<sub>Dsat</sub>)); 0.69 = ln 2; t<sub>p</sub> is in seconds.

head: Method
Formula
Assumption
rows: current approximated by I<sub>Dsat</sub> over the half swing (optimistic)

blocks.text: The two estimates differ by roughly 30%, because one averages current and the other fixes one equivalent resistance. Both are hand estimates; simulation is the reference.

C<sub>L</sub> is rarely one device. It is the sum of four things: drain diffusion capacitance of the nMOS and pMOS, gate-drain overlap capacitance, wire capacitance, and the input capacitance of each fanout gate.

One gate's input capacitance is its gate oxide capacitance plus overlap, for both transistors: C<sub>in</sub> ≈ C<sub>ox</sub>(W<sub>n</sub>L<sub>n</sub> + W<sub>p</sub>L<sub>p</sub>) + overlaps. Doubling the fanout roughly doubles C<sub>L</sub> and so doubles the delay, if the driver current is fixed.

The gate-drain capacitance C<sub>gd</sub> bridges input and output, so it is not a simple load. When the output swings A times as far as the input, the input must supply charge for C<sub>gd</sub>(1 + A). This is the Miller effect.

blocks.where: C<sub>g</sub> is the gate capacitance to the channel, C<sub>gd</sub> is the gate-drain overlap, and A = |dV<sub>out</sub>/dV<sub>in</sub>| in the transition region, typically 5 to 20 for a sharp inverter.

blocks.text: So a switching inverter loads its driver more heavily than a static capacitance measurement suggests. Separately, C<sub>gd</sub> feeds a short spike to the output before the real transition, which appears as a glitch on a dynamic node. No output node is left floating: leakage and charge sharing would make its level undefined.

This sets up the sizing trade-off. A wider driver passes more current but presents more input capacitance to the stage before it; see Chapter 3.4. Delay also trades against the dynamic energy of Chapter 3.5: faster edges mean more short-circuit current.

figure.caption: The input rises at 2 ns and the output reaches its 50% point at 2.5 ns, so t<sub>PHL</sub> = 0.5 ns. The output begins to fall as soon as the input passes V<sub>tn</sub>, but delay is measured at the 50% crossings — here 0.5 ns apart.

examples.question: A CMOS inverter drives C<sub>L</sub> = 50 fF. The nMOS has k<sub>n</sub> = 200 µA/V² and V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.5 V; the supply is V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V. Estimate t<sub>PHL</sub> in nanoseconds.
examples.answer: t<sub>PHL</sub> ≈ 0.27 ns, set by the nMOS discharging 50 fF through about 169 µA.
examples.check:
CL = 50e-15
kn = 200e-6
VDD = 1.8
Vtn = 0.5
Ids = (kn/2)*(VDD-Vtn)**2
Q = CL*VDD/2
t = Q/Ids
print(round(Ids*1e6, 1))
print(round(t*1e9, 4))

code.code:
CL = 50e-15
kn = 200e-6
VDD = 1.8
Vtn = 0.5
Ids = (kn/2)*(VDD-Vtn)**2
t = CL*VDD/(2*Ids)
print(round(Ids*1e6, 1))
print(round(t*1e9, 4))

traps: Swapping t<sub>PHL</sub> and t<sub>PLH</sub>. t<sub>PHL</sub> is the output falling, driven by the nMOS and triggered by a rising input. Examiners check this first.
Dropping the factor 2. Delay ends at the 50% point, so only half the swing is charged; C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>/I<sub>Dsat</sub> doubles the answer.
Using V<sub>DD</sub> instead of the overdrive V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub> inside the square. Current depends on how far above threshold the gate is driven.
Confusing rise time with delay. t<sub>r</sub> is 10% to 90% on the output alone; t<sub>p</sub> is measured between input and output 50% points.
Mixing units. fF × V = fC and µA × ns = fC, so keep fF with µA and read the answer in ns. A 1000× slip is the commonest error here.

quiz.q: Define t<sub>PHL</sub> and name the transistor that sets it.
quiz.a: Time from the input crossing V<sub>DD</sub>/2 while rising to the output crossing V<sub>DD</sub>/2 while falling. The nMOS pull-down sets it.

quiz.q: Between which levels are rise and fall times normally measured?
quiz.a: 10% and 90% of V<sub>DD</sub>. Some texts use 20% and 80%; state which you use.

quiz.q: Why define one number t<sub>p</sub> as the average of two delays?
quiz.a: A gate drives both edges, so a path needs one delay per gate. The average weights the two edges equally, and for a symmetric inverter t<sub>PHL</sub> = t<sub>PLH</sub>, so the average equals either one.

quiz.q: The load capacitance doubles while the transistors stay the same. What happens to t<sub>PHL</sub> and why?
quiz.a: It doubles. Current is unchanged and t = Q/I with Q = C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>/2, so doubling C<sub>L</sub> doubles the charge to be removed.

quiz.q: An nMOS with I<sub>Dsat</sub> = 200 µA drives C<sub>L</sub> = 80 fF at V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V. Estimate t<sub>PHL</sub>.
A driver has R<sub>eq</sub> = 10 kΩ and C<sub>L</sub> = 50 fF. Estimate t<sub>p</sub> with the RC model.
A designer doubles only the pMOS width. Discuss the effect on t<sub>PLH</sub>, t<sub>PHL</sub>, t<sub>p</sub> and input capacitance.
quiz.a: t<sub>PLH</sub> falls because pMOS current roughly doubles. t<sub>PHL</sub> stays almost the same, rising slightly because the larger pMOS adds drain diffusion capacitance. t<sub>p</sub> improves, but by less than half the t<sub>PLH</sub> gain. Input capacitance grows, slowing the driving stage. This is why pMOS width is chosen to match, not to maximise, pull-up strength.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry replaces these formulas with a static timing analyser that reads a Liberty (.lib) timing model per cell at several process, voltage and temperature corners. On-chip variation, ageing and crosstalk are handled by derating factors. In advanced nodes, Miller capacitance and interconnect resistance dominate long nets. Search for static timing analysis, Liberty timing models, PVT corners and Elmore delay for the next layer.
